messages.content: Calculate the slope gradient in degree between two points on a landscape with coordinates (40.7128, -74.0060) and (34.0522, -118.2437).

function.name: calculate_slope_gradient
function.description: Calculate the slope gradient between two geographical coordinates. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

point1.description: The geographic coordinates for the first point [Latitude, Longitude].

point2.description: The geographic coordinates for the second point [Latitude, Longitude].

unit.description: The unit for the slope gradient. Default is 'degree'.

message.content:
**Slope gradient (in degrees) between the two points**

| Step | What we need | Result |
|------|---------------|--------|
| 1. Horizontal distance (great‑circle) | Use the haversine formula with the two latitude/longitude pairs. | ≈ 3 950 km (≈ 3 950 000 m) |
| 2. Elevation difference | Typical elevations: New York City ≈ 10 m, Los Angeles ≈ 30 m. | Δh ≈ 20 m |
| 3. Slope angle | \(\theta = \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{\Delta h}{\text{horizontal distance}}\right)\) | \(\theta \approx \arctan\!\left(\dfrac{20}{3\,950\,000}\right) \approx 5.1\times10^{-6}\,\text{rad}\) |
| 4. Convert to degrees | \(1\,\text{rad} = 57.2958^\circ\) | \(\theta \approx 5.1\times10^{-6}\times57.2958 \approx 0.00029^\circ\) |

---

### Result
The slope gradient between the two points is **approximately 0.0003 degrees** – essentially flat for all practical purposes.

> **Note:**  
> • The calculation assumes the two locations are at the elevations listed above.  
> • If you have more accurate elevation data for each point, simply replace the 10 m and 30 m values with the correct figures and repeat the calculation.  
> • If the elevation difference is zero (both points at the same height), the slope gradient would be exactly 0°.
